feed.title: Re: Safer sighashes and more granular SIGHASH_NOINPUT

entry.title: Re: Safer sighashes and more granular SIGHASH_NOINPUT
entry.summary:
Four distinct levels of knowledge can be distinguished when generating a signature for transaction inputs. The first level, ALL, involves complete awareness of every input associated with the transaction. SINGLE refers to situations where full details are known only about the specific input being signed, leaving other inputs potentially unknown. At the SCRIPTPUBKEY level, there is certainty regarding the exact scriptPubKey that must be satisfied, but not necessarily the transaction ID (txid). The most minimal level, SCRIPTMASK, represents a case where neither the txid, scriptPubKey, nor alternate taproot branches are known; sometimes even certain masked terms within the script remain undisclosed, though the overall structure and unmasked elements are understood.
Masking provides practical benefits primarily in the SCRIPTMASK scenario. Since both the txid and scriptPubKey already encapsulate the full script code, further signing of the script code acts as an additional safeguard rather than fulfilling a critical need. There may be limited scenarios where knowing only the scriptPubKey is genuinely useful, as it is often the case that one will either have access to the txid or require the concealment of some component.
Within the taproot framework, the scriptPubKey is constructed as a point \(P = Q + H(Q,S) \times G\), where \(S\) denotes the Merkle root encompassing potentially many scripts. Spending from this setup can occur through several mechanisms: providing a signature for \(P\), revealing the base point \(Q\), presenting the path through \(S\) and the relevant script, and supplying the witness for the script.
Employing SCRIPTMASK enables the preparation of a signature for a particular script well in advance, even before finalizing the details of other scripts or determining the base point \(Q\). This strategy offers flexibility, allowing certain aspects of the transaction to remain undecided at the time of signature creation, which can lead to improved privacy and modularity in transaction construction.
